# Part 1

**Goal:**   
In Part 1 of this lab, we aim to evaluate the validity of the model of uncertainty propagation. We predict that the model will work and the mass multiplied by the distance to the mass on one side of the pivot will equal the mass multiplied by the distance to the mass on the other side of the pivot. 

**Method:**  
We will attempt to minimize the initial error as best as possible to thus minimize the error propagation.

There is likely some wiggle room in the placement of the meterstick on the pivot point, but given our measuring tools and lab equipment, we think it’s probably fine if we’re within \+/- 0.5cm. The level on the top of the meterstick helps inform us about the level of the meterstick. Given this, we don’t estimate needing to account for the half-cm error on the meterstick positioning.

We want to test if:  
m1\*x1=m2\*x2.  
From an existing physics perspective, we want to validate torques.

We will be computing error propagation through partial derivatives of the form  
𝛿ytotal=√(𝛿y1)2+(𝛿y2)2+...  
Where  
𝛿yi=f'(x)dx  
Per our lab lecture, the total error value is:  
f=i=1n(fzi\*zi)2  
![][image1]  
This computation of our total error allows us to see how much error propagates throughout the experiment, which is what we can use to evaluate the accuracy of our model.

Since we want to check the model in its entirety, we want to check multiple ranges of weights and distance values to see if m1x1= m2x2 no matter what. We are treating the masses as digital measurements, so their error is always going to be \+/- 0.01 gram, while the distance measurements will always be \+/- 0.05cm.

**Data**

The data we collected was across multiple ranges of masses and distances from the center point.

The measurement error on the distance is 0.05cm, or 0.0005 meters; the measurement error on the masses is 0.01g, or 0.00001 kg.

**Conclusion**

The main issue with reducing our uncertainty was just the limits of our measurement devices. If we could further reduce the uncertainty of the measurements, we would drastically reduce our propagated uncertainty due to how the errors are calculated. Since they multiply the measurement error, the smaller the better.

The T-score table is a very good indicator that the torques are balanced properly, i.e. that the model is correct. Our only non-zero T score was the trial between the 100g and 50g mass. We can attribute this non-zero value to both systematic error (us humans measuring), and random error (variations in the masses / measuring devices).

# Part 2

**Goal:**  
In Part 2 of this lab, we aim to determine the mass of an unknown object. We will be using a refined version of the model we analyzed in Part 1\. We predict that the mass of the unknown object will be 80g or less given on physical observations and provided by the bubble lever.

![][image7]  
We will use the above partials in computing the error propagation of this experiment.

**Method**

To identify the unknown mass, we will be moving a 100g weight along the meterstick until the level is balanced. In order to minimize our error, we will redefine the partial derivatives we are using in our error calculations. We fixed the keys at a distance of 30cm from the pivot.

We compute a mass of 82.56g from the equation. The measured mass of the keys was 82.58g. We are within 0.02g of the true value.
